free_tier.stated: Route64 provides the following services to you completely free of charge. Static IPs: 'Need dedicated IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for your services? Route64 offers static IP allocations that remain permanently assigned to your account. Whether you need IPs for web hosting, mail servers, DNS infrastructure, or any other service, our static IPs are geographically flexible and can be deployed across multiple locations. All IP management is handled through our self-service portal.' The pricing block reads 'Pricing? No!' and 'Just created an account in our manager'.
free_tier.notes: The offer is denominated in addresses, a unit this enum does not carry, so the token is none rather than a byte or request unit. The vendor publishes neither a price nor a count of static IPs per account, and no page read on 2026-10-24 states how many addresses one account may hold.

per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: an address, not an object
per_object_cap.notes: An address allocation carries no stored object and therefore no per-object ceiling. The nearest structural cap is the pool: five /24s, 1,280 addresses for the whole service, not a limit on one allocation.

retention.stated: not applicable: a static address, not stored bytes
retention.notes: The page states the allocation 'remain[s] permanently assigned to your account', so there is no idle timer. The ToS at https://route64.org/en/tos bounds it from the other side: 'We can cancel any service at any time without any warning.' Permanence is bounded by the account, not by a clock.

egress.terms: No byte allowance and no traffic price is published for the static-IP product. The nearest published statement is the transit feature block: 'Traffic is not metered and it is possible to get more transit if 200M is not enough.' The ToS adds 'Our service is designed to deliver up to 200M throughput often more.' and 'We can throttle your bandwidth at any time.'

interface_detail: The reachable surface is the self-service web portal at manager.route64.org: 'All IP management is handled through our self-service portal.' No public API or CLI is documented, and manager.route64.org returned a login wall when read. The address is then used directly by the endpoint, or reached over one of the six published tunnel protocols, terminated at the endpoint, so no SOCKS5 or HTTP-proxy protocol is involved. scripts/dossier/schema.json's interface enum has no member for a web portal, a bare address allocation or a tunnel product, so the token is unknown and the qualifier lives here.
tooling: An account in the self-service manager portal is the only published route to an allocation. The address then has to be bound to an existing endpoint, either by placing compute at one of the vendor's PoPs or by terminating one of the six published protocols from it: GRE, GRETAP, SIT, WireGuard, L2TPv3, VXLAN, all listed with both IPv4 and IPv6 endpoints. No proxy wrapper, API client, downloadable configuration or test address is published for the static-IP product, so the announcing AS and the registration class cannot be checked before signing up. A missing wrapper is not a reason to reject this provider: what is missing here is the protocol and the test address, not the wrapper.
chaining: It supplies the Workers gateway with IPv4 source addresses in an ASN that is not AS13335, which is the rung-4 move, and it needs an existing compute endpoint to terminate a tunnel from or to sit at a PoP; it adds address count and one ASN, not registration-class diversity, because every address in the five blocks is IPXO-registered.

limits.value: up to 200 Mbit/s design point: 'Our service is designed to deliver up to 200M throughput often more.'; 'We can throttle your bandwidth at any time.'
none: 'Traffic is not metered' on the transit feature block, and no byte allowance or traffic price is published for the static-IP product

limits_note: No vocabulary kind fits the pool itself. AS212895 announces five IPv4 /24s, which is 1,280 addresses for the whole service, and the vendor's own page claims only '3 IPv4 /24 blocks'. No per-account count of static IPs is published at any tier. The ToS closes the obvious workaround: 'Multiple accounts are not allowed and will cause the suspension of all accounts.'
binding_note: Nothing in the vocabulary fails at the scale: about 45 GB a month across about 599,000 requests averages roughly 0.14 Mbit/s, while the only published throughput ceiling is the 200 Mbit/s design point, which is 2.16 TB a day, and no byte quota exists for the static-IP product. The ceiling that arrives first is structural and unclassified: 1,280 addresses in one ASN and one registration class.

identity_cost.detail: An account in the self-service manager portal is required: 'Just created an account in our manager.' The sign-in page at manager.route64.org returned a login wall to the reader, so the exact fields a new account must supply were not read; email is the minimum such a portal implies and is not confirmed. No card is stated anywhere on the page or the ToS. The ToS adds 'Multiple accounts are not allowed and will cause the suspension of all accounts', so the account is the unit and cannot be multiplied.

reliability_note: Best effort with no SLA ('This is a free best effort service. You have no service levels or guarantees.'); the ToS reserves throttling, nullrouting and cancellation at any time without warning, and one account only; all five blocks are one IPXO registration class and one announcing AS, so a prefix-level blocklist entry or a nullroute removes all 1,280 addresses together.
confidence_note: Autonomous system announcements and RDAP registrations across five /24 subnets were measured via RIPEstat and RDAP on 2026-10-24. Free allocation terms, portal access, and unmetered bandwidth policies are documented from vendor documentation read on 2026-10-24.

evidence.proved: The static-IP offer ('Route64 offers static IP allocations that remain permanently assigned to your account', 'our static IPs are geographically flexible'), the free-of-charge sentence, 'Pricing? No!', the portal account requirement, and the vendor's own count: 'Our address portfolio includes 3 IPv4 /24 blocks and 78 IPv6 /48 blocks.'

AS212895 announces exactly five IPv4 /24s, 81.168.111.0/24, 192.208.1.0/24, 87.229.23.0/24, 81.18.58.0/24 and 79.175.70.0/24, alongside 96 IPv6 prefixes, so the page's '3 IPv4 /24 blocks' is not the current count.

81.18.58.0/24 is originated by AS212895 and seen by 268 of 269 RIS peers; the same query on the same run returned origin 212895 and 268 or 269 peers for 81.168.111.0/24, 192.208.1.0/24, 87.229.23.0/24 and 79.175.70.0/24, so all five are in the DFZ rather than merely registered.

The announcing AS is Route64's own: AS212895 is registered as ROUTE64_ORG, status active, with an individual in Stuttgart, Germany, as registrant. The announcement is therefore not a leased transit AS, which is what separates this case from a transit-only prefix lease.

The registration is not Route64's and is not an ISP's: name IPXO, type SUB-ALLOCATED PA, country EU, registrant ORG-PC1552-RIPE, administrative, technical and abuse contact PC21176-RIPE 'Private Customer', remark 'End User Organization'. The same query returned IPXO-LEASED-81-168-111-0-24 for 81.168.111.0/24, HGC-Global-Communications-Limited with IPXO details for 87.229.23.0/24, and IPXO with type ASSIGNED PA for 79.175.70.0/24.

The fifth block is registered in a different registry and reads differently: ARIN handle NET-192-208-1-0-4, type ASSIGNMENT, parent NET-192-208-1-0-3, registrant C11060843 'Private Customer', with a remark pointing at the vendor's geofeed. No IPXO name appears on it, so the five blocks are not one uniform registration.

The vendor declares location per sub-block inside single /24s: a /28 in Stockholm, a /29 in London, /31s in Paris, Zurich and Frankfurt, all inside 79.175.70.0/24. The country an address appears in is vendor-published, not a registry fact, and RDAP still reads EU for that block.

The published ceilings and the reliability position: 'Our service is designed to deliver up to 200M throughput often more.', 'We can throttle your bandwidth at any time.', 'We can cancel any service at any time without any warning.', 'We can nullroute your advertised prefixes at any time without any warning.', 'This is a free best effort service. You have no service levels or guarantees.', 'Multiple accounts are not allowed and will cause the suspension of all accounts.'

price_per_tb_month: USD 0: the allocation and its traffic are both free, and no per-byte price exists at any tier
notes:
Network structure and registration classification for Route64 static IPv4 allocations. Vendor documentation describes static IP allocations assigned permanently to user accounts without making residential or eyeball ISP claims.

Routing and registration analysis on 2026-10-24: BGP routing queries in RIPEstat show five /24 blocks (1,280 total addresses) announced by AS212895 (ROUTE64_ORG) and visible to over 268 RIS peers, exceeding the three /24 blocks stated in website text. Registration records show four blocks sub-allocated from IPXO (PA space under ORG-PC1552-RIPE) and a fifth block under ARIN Private Customer assignment. These represent commercial IP lease pools rather than residential eyeball networks.

Geofeed fragmentation: published geofeed records assign sub-delegations across multiple European countries (such as /28 in Stockholm, /29 in London, and /31s in Paris, Zurich, and Frankfurt) while parent RDAP objects maintain EU regional assignments.

extras.rung_note: Five /24s originated by AS212895 clear rung 3, an address in a different /24, and rung 4, a network that is not AS13335; rung 5 is not cleared, because all five blocks are IPXO sub-allocations reading 'Private Customer'.
extras.vendor_claimed_v4_blocks: 3 IPv4 /24 blocks (page text, 2026-10-24), against five announced
extras.registration: IPXO or IPXO-LEASED on four blocks, SUB-ALLOCATED PA or ASSIGNED PA, country EU, ORG-PC1552-RIPE, contact PC21176-RIPE 'Private Customer', remark 'End User Organization'; ARIN ASSIGNMENT NET-192-208-1-0-4 to C11060843 'Private Customer' on the fifth
extras.geofeed_note: single /24s are carved into per-country fragments, so the declared country is vendor-published and not a registry fact
extras.transit_cap: 200 Mbit/s design point, throttle at any time
extras.derivation: 1,280 addresses is 5 x 256, arithmetic on the five /24s RIPEstat returned; 0.14 Mbit/s is 45 GB over 30 days; 2.16 TB/day is 200 Mbit/s. None of the three is a measurement.
extras.verification_gap: no address was delivered, so whether a delivered static IP is one of these five blocks, and whether it egresses from AS212895 as a usable exit, is unmeasured
extras.duplicate_of: dossier/egress/route64-org.json owns the IPv6 /56 tunnel product; this record owns IPv4 static allocation only
